B: Hello, can you hear me? Sorry, I'm, er, I'm in the spare room, the lamp's doing something weird.
A: Yeah, I can hear you fine, mate. Gareth. You're looking all right, don't worry.
B: Karim. Nice to meet you, Gareth. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start?
A: I did, yeah. Erm, I got about halfway and then sort of stared at it. Wordle's more my level, to be honest. My wife's got me doing it every morning.
B: [laughs] Same. I just kept moving the pieces round hoping it'd sort itself out. That's basically how I do my job as well, so.
A: Go on then, what is your job?
B: So I'm commercial director at a food import company in Smethwick. Middle Eastern, Mediterranean stuff. We bring it in and sell it on to independent shops and restaurants round the Midlands. My bit is basically spotting what's going to sell before everyone else does, and then talking buyers into it. My car is literally full of samples right now. There's about forty jars of pomegranate molasses rolling round the boot.
A: [laughs] That sounds like a better car than mine. Mine's full of muddy wellies and a brushcutter.
B: Brushcutter? What do you do?
A: I'm a countryside ranger, er, senior ranger, for the council up in Darwen. So it's moorland paths, bit of woodland, a reservoir walk, school visits. I've got two rangers under me and a load of volunteers. Saw a pair of stonechats this morning on the moor, actually, so it's been a good day.
B: Stonechats. I wouldn't know one if it landed on me, to be honest.
A: Little brown bird, the male's got a black head and an orangey chest. Makes a noise like two stones knocking together, hence the name. Sorry, I'll stop. I get going on birds.
B: No, no, I like that. That's the kind of thing I'd look up later and then go down a hole for an hour. Is that the tower in your photo? On the hill behind you?
A: Jubilee Tower, yeah. On Darwen Hill. You can see it from half of Lancashire.
B: I do phone photography, mostly buildings. I'd have a go at that. Big old stone thing on a hill, that's right up my street.
A: You'd be welcome. There's a decent pub at the bottom an' all, that's the main thing. Do you get out walking much yourself?
B: Honestly? No. I'm in the car between suppliers most of the week. I play five-a-side on a Tuesday when I remember my trainers, and we lose. Every week. We lost again last night.
A: [laughs] I played Sunday league till my forties. My knees still haven't forgiven me. Who do you follow?
B: Villa. Since ninety-five, a mate dragged me to Villa Park. You?
A: Rovers. Blackburn. Don't ask about Saturday, we were rubbish.
B: I won't ask. [laughs] Are you from round there originally?
A: Born and bred in Blackburn. My dad was a fitter at the paper mill. Proper mill town lad, me. What about you, are you Birmingham born?
B: No, I came over from Basra, in Iraq, when I was fourteen. Bit of a time in Jordan first. So I'm a Brummie when I'm abroad and an Iraqi when someone in Birmingham asks where I'm really from.
A: [laughs] That's a good answer, that. I might pinch that.
B: Go for it. My dad used to say something like it, actually. He passed in 2016. I wish I'd asked him a lot more, you know, about his life back there.
A: Yeah. Mine as well, he went a few years back. You always think there's time, don't you.
B: You do. Anyway, what's your lunch situation? Because I eat egg baps from the café by the warehouse basically every day.
A: A barm from the bakery by the depot. Had one today.
B: Barm. See, that's the same thing, that's a bap.
A: It's a barm, pal, I'm not having it.
